subject: nigerian-history
title: Important historical sites in Nigeria

curriculum.note: Primary 4, Third Term: “Important historical features and sites in Nigeria” appears in a published scheme of work that says it follows the new NERDC curriculum. It has not been checked against the official NERDC document.

introduction: Long ago, people in the land we now call Nigeria made beautiful things from clay and metal, built towns and farmed on hills. Some of the places where they lived and worked are still here today. We call them **historical sites**.
In this lesson you will visit six of these places on a map and find out what was found there.
why: Historical sites help us to know how people lived before us. They are part of the heritage that all Nigerians share and must protect.
objectives: say what a historical site is
name and find six important historical sites in Nigeria on a map
say one thing that each site is known for
explain why we should protect historical sites

blocks.text: A **historical site** is a place where people lived, worked, worshipped or made things a long time ago. Old walls, palaces, sacred groves and places where old objects were dug up can all be historical sites.
People called **archaeologists** study these places. They dig carefully and study what they find, such as pots, tools and sculptures, to learn about the past.
Some old objects are very fragile. If you ever find something very old in the ground, tell an adult so that experts can look after it.

sections.title: Places where wonderful art was made

blocks.caption: Six historical sites in Nigeria
blocks.credit: World Explorer map. Nigeria outline: Natural Earth (public domain). The map shows modern Nigeria; site positions are approximate.

items.title: Nok (Kaduna State)
items.text: Clay (terracotta) heads and figures. The first was found in 1943 during tin mining near the village of Nok. The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates Nok terracottas to about 500 BC–AD 200, more than 2,000 years ago. The Nok people also worked iron.

items.title: Igbo-Ukwu (Anambra State)
items.text: Bronze objects with very fine patterns. A farmer, Isaiah Anozie, found the first ones in 1938 while digging near his home. They were made about 1,100 years ago, in the 800s AD.

items.title: Ile-Ife (Osun State)
items.text: Life-like heads made of copper alloy and terracotta. A famous head found in 1938 is thought to have been made about 600 to 700 years ago.

items.title: Benin City (Edo State)
items.text: Brass plaques that once decorated the Oba’s palace, showing people and events at the royal court. Many were made in the 1500s and 1600s. In 1897 British soldiers took many of them away.

blocks.text: Some places are so important that UNESCO lists them as **World Heritage Sites**, to be protected for everyone. Nigeria has two:

items.title: Sukur Cultural Landscape (Adamawa State), listed in 1999
items.text: On a hill in the Mandara Mountains: the stone palace of the Hidi (the chief), farm terraces cut into the hillside, and the remains of old iron-smelting furnaces. It was the first cultural landscape in Africa to be listed.

items.title: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (Osun State), listed in 2005
items.text: A forest at Osogbo that is a shrine to Osun, the Yoruba goddess of fertility. From the 1950s, the artist Susanne Wenger and local artists made large sculptures there. It is one of the last areas of original high forest in southern Nigeria.

items: They show us how people lived, worked and believed long ago.
They are part of our heritage: they belong to all of us and to the children who come after us.
Visitors come to see them, which helps the local community.
Once a site or object is damaged or taken away, it can never be the same again.

blocks.text: Museums such as the National Museum in Lagos look after objects from historical sites so that everyone can learn from them.

activities.title: Explore the sites on the map
activities.instructions: Choose a site to see where it is today, when it is from and what was found there.

items.title: Nok
items.subtitle: Kaduna State
facts: About 500 BC–AD 200 (more than 2,000 years ago; experts still study the exact dates)
Terracotta (clay) sculptures, signs of iron working
items.text: Nok sculptures often have large heads and carefully made eyes, ears and hair.

items.title: Igbo-Ukwu
items.subtitle: Anambra State
facts: Bronze objects with fine patterns, and beads
items.text: Archaeologist Thurstan Shaw dug there carefully in 1959 and found more objects.

items.title: Ile-Ife
items.subtitle: Osun State
facts: Life-like heads of copper alloy and terracotta
items.text: One famous head, found in 1938, is now in the British Museum in London.

items.title: Benin City
items.subtitle: Edo State
facts: Many plaques were made in the 1500s and 1600s
Brass plaques from the Oba’s palace
items.text: The plaques show the Oba, chiefs, soldiers and visitors, including Portuguese traders.

items.title: Sukur
items.subtitle: Adamawa State
facts: The Hidi’s stone palace, farm terraces, old iron furnaces
items.text: Sukur was the first cultural landscape in Africa on the World Heritage List.

items.title: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
items.subtitle: Osun State
facts: Sacred forest, shrines and large sculptures
items.text: The grove is the largest surviving shrine to Osun, the Yoruba goddess of fertility.

activities.instructions: For each site, choose what it is known for. Then press Check.

questions.q: Match each site to what it is known for.
pairs: Brass plaques from the Oba’s palace
Hill palace, farm terraces and iron furnaces
questions.explain: Nok is known for terracotta, Igbo-Ukwu for bronzes, Benin for its palace plaques and Sukur for its hill landscape.

activities.title: Put these in order, oldest first
activities.instructions: Move the items up or down until the oldest is at the top. Then press Check.

questions.q: Put these in time order, oldest first.
items: Nok terracottas are made (about 2,000 years ago)
Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are made (about 1,100 years ago)
The famous Ife head is made (about 600–700 years ago)
Sukur becomes a World Heritage Site (1999)
Osun-Osogbo Grove becomes a World Heritage Site (2005)
questions.explain: Nok is the oldest. The first three dates are approximate (“about”), because experts work them out from evidence. 1999 and 2005 are exact dates, because they were written down when they happened.

key_terms: A place where people lived, worked, worshipped or made things long ago.
A person who studies the past by carefully digging up and examining old objects and places.
Clay that has been shaped and baked hard.
A metal made by mixing copper with another metal such as tin.
Things from the past that we value and pass on: places, objects, customs and stories.
A place that UNESCO lists as so important that it should be protected for all people.
summary: A historical site is a place where people lived, worked, worshipped or made things long ago.
Nok is famous for terracotta sculptures, Igbo-Ukwu for bronzes, Ile-Ife for life-like heads and Benin for palace plaques.
Nigeria’s two World Heritage Sites are Sukur (1999) and the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (2005).
Some dates are exact; others are “about”, worked out from evidence.
Historical sites are our shared heritage, so we must protect them.

options.text: A place where people lived or made things long ago
options.why: Yes: historical sites tell us about the past.
A new building is not from long ago.
Rivers are natural features; a historical site is linked to people in the past.

assessment.q: Look at the map. Which site is marker 1?

options.why: Yes: marker 1 is Nok, in the middle of the country (Kaduna State).
Benin City is marker 5, in the south.
Sukur is marker 6, far to the east near Cameroon.

assessment.q: Look at the map again. Which marker shows Sukur?

options.why: Yes: Sukur is in Adamawa State in the north-east, near Cameroon.
Marker 2 is Igbo-Ukwu in Anambra State.
Marker 3 is Ile-Ife in Osun State.

assessment.statement: The Igbo-Ukwu bronzes were first found by a farmer digging near his home.
assessment.explain: Isaiah Anozie found the first bronzes in 1938 while digging near his home.

assessment.statement: Nigeria has five World Heritage Sites.
assessment.explain: Nigeria has two: Sukur Cultural Landscape (1999) and the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (2005).

assessment.text: Clay that is shaped and baked hard is called ___.
assessment.explain: Nok sculptures are made of terracotta.

assessment.q: Why do we say the Nok sculptures are “about” 2,000 years old?

options.text: Because experts work out the age from evidence, so it is not an exact date
options.why: Yes: nobody wrote down the date, so experts estimate it.

options.text: Because nobody knows anything about Nok
options.why: We know quite a lot from the sculptures and the places they were found.

options.text: Because the sculptures were made last year
options.why: They are very old, not new.

assessment.situation: On a school trip to a historical site, a classmate wants to scratch their name on an old wall.

options.text: Ask them kindly not to, and tell the teacher if they continue
options.why: This protects the site and keeps everyone safe.
This encourages damage to something that cannot be replaced.
Staying out of trouble is understandable, but the wall may still be damaged.

assessment.explain: Historical sites belong to everyone. Once damaged, they cannot be the same again.

assessment.prompt: In one or two sentences, say why we should protect historical sites.
assessment.model: We should protect historical sites because they show us how people lived long ago and they are part of the heritage we share and pass on.
points: Mentions heritage or sharing with others
Gives a clear reason in a full sentence
